title: UPSTYLE_Backdoor_Investigation_d1c
description: Your organization has detected suspicious activity on one of its Linux servers. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor named UPSTYLE. Your task is to investigate, analyze, and respond to this cybersecurity incident.
outcomes: Identify and investigate unauthorized or suspicious services running on a host.
Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.
Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: Your organization has detected suspicious activity on one of its Linux servers. Initial analysis suggests the presence of a backdoor named UPSTYLE. Your task is to investigate, analyze, and respond to this cybersecurity incident.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host via SSH using the username 'user' and password 'password'. Enter 'start' to proceed.
levels.local_content: Access the target host via SSH using the username 'user' and password 'password'. Enter 'start' to proceed.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the network, you noticed unusual outbound connections from the target host. Investigate the running services on the target host to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any services that seem out of place or unfamiliar. The suspicious service in this case is `bkd.service`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the list of running services and look for any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you have identified the suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after a system reboot. This will help you understand the persistence mechanism used by the attacker.
levels.solution: To determine how the suspicious service is automatically started, you can use the `systemctl list-timers` command to list all systemd timers. Look for any timers that are associated with the suspicious service. The systemd timer responsible for starting the suspicious service in this case is `lab-checkin.timer`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate the systemd services and timers to find how the suspicious service is started.

levels.title: Suspicious File Discovery
levels.content: Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service. This will help you gather more information about the backdoor and its behavior.
levels.solution: To locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl cat bkd.service` command to view the service unit file. The path to the executable associated with the suspicious service in this case is `/usr/local/bin/lab-checkin.sh`.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the service unit file to find the path to the executable.
